tool.name: ExtractAspectValuesToPoints
tool.summary: Copies the input point features and adds a field holding the aspect value at each point, extracted from an aspect raster -- like Esri's Extract Values to Points, but built for aspect: the optional interpolation is a bilinear weighted mean direction (a circular interpolation, never a linear average), flat cells (-1) are handled correctly, D-infinity flow-direction rasters are supported, and no Spatial Analyst is required.
tool.usage:
Why a special tool for aspect. Aspect is a circular variable: 0 and 360 degrees are the same direction, and 359 and 1 are two degrees apart. An ordinary interpolated extraction (such as Esri's Extract Values to Points with interpolation on) averages the neighboring cell values linearly, so a point between a 359-degree cell and a 1-degree cell would get roughly 180 -- due south, the exact opposite of the correct roughly-north answer. This tool instead treats each neighboring cell as a unit vector and computes a bilinear weighted mean direction: the sines and cosines of the four surrounding cell centers are weighted by the standard bilinear weights, summed, and converted back to a direction. The result is always a true direction in compass degrees. (See the tool help for the Aspect Focal Statistics tool, and Jenness, J. 2012, "Directions: making sense of directional data," for why aspect matters ecologically and why circular methods are required.)
Extraction options. With interpolation off (the default, matching Esri's default) each point receives the value of the raster cell it falls in, exactly as stored -- including -1 for a flat cell. With interpolation on, each point receives the weighted mean direction of the four surrounding cell centers as described above. Flat cells (aspect -1) carry no direction, so they are excluded from the interpolation and the weights are renormalized over the remaining directional neighbors; if every contributing neighbor is flat the point receives -1; NoData neighbors are likewise excluded. Points on NoData or outside the raster receive NULL in a geodatabase output, or -9999 in a shapefile (which cannot store null). The tool warns if the raster's values fall outside the aspect range (-1 to 360 degrees), which usually means the input is not an aspect raster.
Output. The output is a new point feature class: a copy of the input points (an active selection is honored) carrying all the input attributes plus one new DOUBLE field (default name "Aspect"; the name is adjusted if invalid or already taken) holding the extracted value in compass degrees. Esri's option to append all the raster's attributes is deliberately not offered. The field's metadata records the units, the -1 and NULL/-9999 conventions, the extraction method, and the source raster.
Coordinate systems. The points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected -- projecting a raster damages it; reprojecting point coordinates is exact), and the raster is read only over the points' extent, so large regional rasters are handled efficiently. Projected and geographic rasters both work.
D-infinity flow direction. A D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster is essentially an aspect raster -- the direction of steepest descent -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise) rather than compass, which most users do not realize. Set "Input aspect convention" to Mathematical for such a raster and the extracted values are converted to compass degrees. The tool suggests this setting automatically when it detects a DINF raster from the geoprocessing history. (A standard D8 flow-direction raster stores flow codes 1-128, not degrees, and is not valid input.)
Values are always written in compass degrees (0 = north, clockwise); -1 = flat. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments. References: circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); see also Jenness (2012).

dialogReference.para: The point features to extract aspect values for. An active selection is honored. Must be a single-point feature class (multipoint is not supported).

A single-band aspect raster in degrees, 0-360 measured clockwise from north (compass), with -1 for flat cells. A D-infinity flow-direction raster is also valid input -- set the Input aspect convention to Mathematical for it. The tool warns if the values fall outside the -1 to 360 range (probably not an aspect raster).
The new point feature class: a copy of the input points with all their attributes plus the new aspect field. A name is suggested from the input.

param.name: interpolate
param.displayname: Interpolate values at the point locations (weighted mean direction)

dialogReference.para: Unchecked (default): each point gets the value of the cell it falls in, exactly as stored (including -1 for flat). Checked: each point gets a bilinear weighted mean direction interpolated from the four surrounding cell centers -- a circular interpolation in which each neighbor's direction is treated as a unit vector, so directions near north interpolate correctly (359 and 1 give roughly 0, never 180). Flat and NoData neighbors are excluded and the weights renormalized; all-flat neighbors give -1.
The name of the new DOUBLE field holding the extracted aspect (default "Aspect"). Adjusted automatically if the name is invalid for the output workspace or already taken.

The angular convention of the input raster. Choose Compass for an ordinary aspect raster (0 = north, increasing clockwise). Choose Mathematical for a D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster: DINF reports the direction of steepest descent -- essentially aspect -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise), which most users do not realize. With Mathematical selected the extracted values are converted to compass degrees. The tool suggests this setting automatically when it detects a DINF raster.

scriptExample.title: Extract Aspect Values to Points example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Extract the containing-cell aspect, then a circular-interpolated aspect. interpolate: True or False. input_convention: "Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", "Mathematical (0 = east, counter-clockwise; e.g. D-infinity)". The new field is DOUBLE, compass degrees; -1 = flat; NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile) = NoData or outside the raster.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Value of the cell each point falls in (no interpolation) arcpy.jenness.ExtractAspectValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", out_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points_Aspect", interpolate=False, field_name="Aspect", input_convention="Compass (0 = north, clockwise)")
# Circular (weighted mean direction) interpolation from the 4 nearest cells arcpy.jenness.ExtractAspectValuesToPoints( in_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points", in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", out_points=r"C:\Project\Wildlife.gdb\telemetry_points_AspInterp", interpolate=True, field_name="Aspect")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Copies point features and adds a field with the aspect at each point from an aspect raster -- containing-cell value or bilinear weighted-mean-direction (circular) interpolation; flat (-1) handled correctly; D-infinity supported; no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: The circular analog of Esri's Extract Values to Points. Aspect is a circular variable, so an ordinary interpolated extraction averages neighboring values linearly and puts ~180 between 359 and 1; this tool instead computes a bilinear WEIGHTED MEAN DIRECTION (unit vectors of the four surrounding cell centers, bilinearly weighted, resultant converted back to a direction). Flat cells (aspect -1) are excluded from interpolation with weights renormalized; all-flat neighbors give -1; NoData or outside-the-raster points get NULL (geodatabase) or -9999 (shapefile). Points are read in the raster's coordinate system (the raster is never projected) and the raster is read only over the points' extent. D-infinity flow-direction rasters -- essentially aspect in the mathematical convention -- are supported via a convention toggle that converts values to compass. All input attributes are carried; one new DOUBLE field is added with full field-level metadata. Circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); see Jenness (2012).

Statistical Analysis of Circular Data (Cambridge Univ. Press); Batschelet, E. 1981. Circular Statistics in Biology (Academic Press); Zar, J. H. 1999. Biostatistical Analysis, 4th ed. (Prentice Hall). See also Jenness, J. 2012, "Directions: making sense of directional data" (Jenness Enterprises). Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Extract Aspect Values to Points.
